articles.title: Robert Pattinson's James Bond Will Make Movie History By Changing 1 Word From the Rest of the Franchise
articles.summary: White smoke has emerged from MGM as a new James Bond has officially been revealed, with Robert Pattinson taking on the iconic role. The times are a-changing, though, because in years past the christening of a new 007 would have been a major event. Thanks to the character's cultural status in the UK, massive press […]
articles.content:
Not only will Pattinson be taking on the part and bringing a new performance to the character after his announcement was distinct, but the team behind the scenes is different too. After ousting Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, Amazon MGM has put Amy Pascal and David Heyman behind the series as its producers . Perhaps the biggest change that James Bond 26 will make is a subtle one, though; it's just a one-word change that will be different from every other movie in the entire film franchise, and it's all about who James Bond is working for: The King.

Queen Elizabeth II began her reign as the monarch of the UK on February 6, 1952, just one year before the publication of the first James Bond novel, Casino Royale , and ten years prior to the first James Bond movie, Dr. No . That means that for the entirety of James Bond's life as a fictional character in books and feature films, his career as a secret agent working for MI6 has been described with five words. These five words even became the title of one of the books and one of the best movies in the series: “ On Her Majesty's Secret Service .”

On September 8, 2022, eleven months after the release of Daniel Craig's final James Bond movie, No Time to Die , Queen Elizabeth II passed away and was succeeded by her son, making him King Charles III. As a result, when Robert Pattinson's James Bond makes his debut, he'll not only be the first Bond from a new creative regime, but he'll be the first ever to work “On His Majesty's Secret Service.” This one-word change may not seem like a big deal in the slightest to some, but the fact that the change has been made at all speaks to not only the length of Elizabeth's reign but how much it has defined things, even pop culture like James Bond's career.

It's worth noting that Robert Pattinson's James Bond will be the first movie in the series to acknowledge this change to UK politics, but it's technically not the first Bond story to do so. Earlier this year, the 007: First Light video game that arrived to critical acclaim back in May did the same thing. All that in mind, though, Pattinson being referred to with a job title that no other big-screen Bond has been given will immediately differentiate him from what's come before. Beyond that subtle change, it remains to be seen how different the new film will be from what has come before it, but small details beget even bigger changes, and we could be in store for something distinct with the new Bond.

articles.summary: Image Courtesy of Netflix The X-Men casting rumors are continuing, and there is a new name being thrown around for the role of Mystique. According to rumors, Marvel wants to cast Victoria Pedretti as the mutant villain. Before this, Rebecca Romijn played Mystique in the original trilogy of X-Men movies, and then Jennifer Lawrence took on the role in […]
articles.content:
According to scooper James Mack, actress Victoria Pedretti is in the running for the role of Mystique in the MCU's X-Men reboot, and she is Marvel Studios' top choice. Most fans will recognize Pedretti from her roles in the Netflix horror series The Haunting of Hill House and The Haunting of Bly Manor . She also starred in the Netflix thriller series You .

Victoria Pedretti is reportedly in the running for the role of MYSTIQUE in the MCU, and she is apparently Marvel Studios’ top choice for the role! 📰: @JamesMackwl pic.twitter.com/81YsGLgFUI

Victoria Pedretti had her breakout role on The Haunting of Hill House , the Mike Flanagan miniseries based on the Shirley Jackson novel. She played Nell on the series, and she quickly made her name in the horror genre. She played Love Quinn in the thriller series You , and then she took on the main role of Dani in the next Flanagan miniseries, The Haunting of Bly Manor . She debuted on the big screen with a supporting role in Quentin Tarantino's Once Upon a Time in Hollywood . Now, she could have a chance at the biggest movie role of her career.

Pedretti is 31, and even though she is only six years older than Inde Navarrette , the MCU probably won't need to change the relationship between her and Rogue. In the comics, Mystique is very old, but thanks to her shapeshifting mutant powers, she is able to look as young as she wants. In the comics, Mystique is the mother of Nightcrawler. Along with her partner Destiny, she is also the adoptive mother of Rogue. Rogue and Mystique both appeared in the original X-Men trilogy, and their relationship was never in play, so it might not happen in the MCU either.

It should be noted that Hunter Schafer has also been rumored for the role . That said, adding an actress of Pedretti's caliber to the role of Mystique could be a great decision by Marvel Studios. She has proven to be a solid ensemble actor and has held her own every step of the way. She won an MTV Movie & TV Award for her performance in The Haunting of Bly Manor and has been nominated at the Saturn Awards, Hollywood Critics Association Awards, and the Critics' Choice Super Awards. Adding her to the MCU could really help the X-Men's impressive cast get even better.

articles.title: Attack on Titan Doesn't Need a Comeback After Its Perfect Ending
articles.summary: Image Courtesy of MAPPA Despite fan backlash during the manga's serialization, it's pretty obvious at this point that Attack on Titan already has a perfect ending. When it comes to anime series released in the 2010s and 2020s, their legacy can't be matched by anything else. In fact, the controversy at the time was so intense that Hajime Isayama, […]
articles.content:
Established in 2011, MAPPA is known as one of the most renowned animation studios in Japan. While its popularity skyrocketed in the 2020s with the release of Jujutsu Kaisen and a few other acclaimed shows, the studio had a strong foundation with exceptional shows and movies under its belt ever since its establishment. Fans naturally had high expectations from the studio for the final season, especially since the time-skip changed the entire narrative. MAPPA not only lived up to the expectations, but delivered the best possible version of the story in the final season and special episodes. The anime reached its conclusion on November 4th, 2023, with the release of the second special episode of Attack on Titan: Final Season – The Final Chapters .

The final stretch of the manga sparked numerous controversies with nuanced scenes that not many appreciated, as well as the death of beloved characters. The ending became less hated despite having reasonable detractors after the anime adaptation , since a few years had passed by then, and the original scenes soothed fans’ disappointment. The problem with cynical or analytical endings is that not everyone will perceive them in the same way. Additionally, Mikasa kissing Eren’s severed head should’ve been an emotional moment of the story, but it didn’t have the impact it should’ve because of its off-putting execution.

The cycle never truly ended in the series, leaving room for a sequel or a spin-off, but the creator has yet to return with a new story. Several decades after Eren’s death, Paradis is still destroyed, and a young boy with a dog discovers the tree where Eren was buried, which now has the same appearance as the tree where Ymir gained the power of the Titans. The implication is that the boy may gain the abilities of a Titan, thereby bringing that destructive power into the world again. Hence, there’s a strong possibility that the current world remains at risk of going through everything all over again, implying that peace is not everlasting.

Considering how much fans hated the finale when the manga was being serialized, not many expected that the controversy would completely die down after the anime adaptation. Isayama was also involved in the production and worked closely with the anime staff to refine dialogue and certain moments while subtly adding original scenes. He also helped tweak many scenes to make the emotional beats land more sincerely than they did in the manga. The anime didn’t make major changes from the original, but these minor details and the presentation with stunning animation made a world of difference.

This not only made fans forget their initial dissatisfaction with the manga, but also helped the series reach new heights of global popularity. The anime was well-received thanks to all the efforts of the studio and the creator. Despite taking the torch from WIT Studio during a controversial moment and the tight deadlines, MAPPA’s adaptation saved the series with one of the best adaptations in recent years. Since Isayama didn’t work on any extra chapter or spin-off, there won’t be another anime episode or movie with a completely new story.

However, that doesn’t mean the end of the franchise since both WIT Studio and MAPPA keep returning with new projects and merchandise to keep fans intrigued.Its final chapters drive home its powerful — albeit bleak — message about the cycle of violence and human nature. And it gives the series and its characters an epic send-off from the beginning of Season 4. There’s tons of well-animated action, along with great callbacks to prior chapters and incredible character growth. It’s everything you could want in a finale, and it doesn’t deserve all the hate it gets.

Do you think MAPPA delivered the perfect ending for Attack on Titan ? What moment from the finale made the biggest impression on you? Share your thoughts in the comments below!

articles.title: 'The Fantasticks' Review: A Welcome Broadway Debut Seven Decades In The Making
articles.summary: Two trunks for storing theatrical props share the stage early in the new production of The Fantasticks, opening for the first time ever on Broadway tonight. One is "Hayes Theater" and the other "Sullivan Street Playhouse," as clear a mission statement as any fan of this stalwart of '60s whimsy could want. With a new […]
articles.content:
Two trunks for storing theatrical props share the stage early in the new production of The Fantasticks , opening for the first time ever on Broadway tonight. One is “Hayes Theater” and the other “Sullivan Street Playhouse,” as clear a mission statement as any fan of this stalwart of '60s whimsy could want.

With a new approach that reimagines the musical's star-crossed boy-meets-girl plot for a boy-meets-boy world, this revival directed by Christopher Gattelli arrives in the 21st Century with both a fresh attitude and a devotion to the spirit of a work that all but defined Off Broadway charm nearly 70 years ago. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News Bryan Cranston & Marianne Jean-Baptiste Heading To Broadway In Ivo Van Hove's Acclaimed 'All My Sons' Revival News 'Downstate' Broadway Review: Provocative Play About Sex Offenders Questions The Nature Of Forgiveness

Granted, that's a charm that might well be lost on some audiences today, much the way Pippin and Godspell could seem impossibly twee in a Broadway where Downstate just opened and a dance club take on Shakespeare has New Yorkers lining up outside the Winter Garden. Then again, this is also a Broadway where the very sweet Two Strangers (Carry A Cake Across New York ) held on longer than anyone imagined . Gattelli and his fine cast of newcomers and veterans know perfectly well what they're up to – and up against, staying faithful to the winsomeness that kept The Fantasticks running Off Broadway for a total 42 years (!). They know that abandoning the ingratiating amiability and theater-kid appeal of this Tom Jones-Harvey Schmidt musical that gave early breaks to Jerry Orbach and many generations of soon-to-be stars would be like cutting “Try To Remember” from the score.

No small part of this revival's pleasures are the coming together of relative newcomers – Maxim Chlumecky and Nathan Levy as the two boys, Fire Island ‘s Zane Phillips making an impressive Broadway debut as El Gallo – with beloved stage figures Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer and Ruthie Ann Miles (as the mothers). They're all terrific singers with crowd-pleasing comic skills – Kritzer and Miles perform a splendid song-and-dance number, “Never Say No,” early in the show – and their matched by a supporting cast that includes David Patrick Kelly, Kevin del Aguila and Ahmad Simmons. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The musical's lovely score, including the stand-out “Try To Remember” as well as once-familiar songs like “Much More,” “Soon It's Gonna Rain” and “I Can See It” that crossed over to wider audiences when Barbra Streisand and others covered them back when the stage was a routine conduit to pop charts, retains its appeal (even if purists might sniff at Sam Davis' appealing new orchestrations that add strings, woodwinds and some brass to the famously minimalist piano and harp sound of the original production and its 1960 cast album.

So, the plot – and keep in mind it falls somewhere between allegory and fairy tale, with a touch of the foolery and disguised motivations of Shakespearean comedy tossed in, and never quite matching its intended heights much less its sources. The two youths – Matt and Luisa in the original, Matt and Lewis here – are nextdoor neighbors, in love and pining but secretly, lest their feuding parents – fathers in the original, mothers here – demand a cease and desist.

Unbeknownst to the boys, the parents are actually great friends, and merely invented the fake feud to push the sons together. As the moms sing in the ode to reverse psychology “Never Say No,” “Dog's got to bark, a mule's got to bray/Soldiers must fight and preachers must pray/And children, I guess, must get their own way/The minute that you say no.”

The parents further conspire to recruit the famous magician, El Gallo, and two itinerant actors to fake-abduct Lewis so that Matt can play the hero and seal the lovers' happy ending. All goes as planned, until the moonlit bliss of Act I gives way to the buyer's remorse of Act II. The boys long for freedom – from one another – and the mothers descend to bickering and frayed nerves.

Another happy ending, older and wiser, eventually arrives, and here, as always, the musical's increasingly cloying second act drags and strains under its own contrivances. Gattelli, with the same know-how he brought to Schmigadoon! and Death Becomes Her , goes quite a way in almost making us overlook the musical's weaknesses, and he's helped by his really game cast (Chlumecky, as Matt, the more boyishly adventuresome of the boys, steals just about every scene he's in).

Gattelli's restrained choreography, including some full-on dance numbers but just as often simpler movement and joyful bounding, works well with the minimalist traditions of the show, which extend to Jason Sherwood's set design (the usual brick theater backdrop, a cut-out crescent moon, wheeled-in window frames now and then, a sweet flowering of greenery and starlight at the right moment) and Linda Cho's costumes that blend the boys' normcore with the showily sexy bandit flash of El Gallo.

As is this show's custom, the wall that's erected by the parents to keep the kids faux-apart is played by a silent actor (Ahmad Simmons, in concrete-gray formalwear and stovepipe hat) who stands between the two households (each side represented by a small plot of vegetation, flowers on one side, veggies on the other).

In this production, that character retains the traditional billing as “The Mute,” a dated term that here survives, unlike the original's use of the word “rape” that, even in 1960, was an archaic synonym for “abduction” (as in Alexander Pope's 1712 poem “The Rape of the Lock”). Here, as in most productions of the musical, they make the wise decision to just say abduction. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-articleX","mid-article","btf","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() ; });

Even without doing a word-for-word comparison of the original Tom Jones (no, not that Tom Jones) lyrics and the ones he revised for this version shortly before his death in 2023 , the musical supports the gender-switch with remarkable ease. Levy portrays Lewis (née Luisa) with a disarming celebration of guilelessness and an ingénue's “I feel pretty” self-infatuation. The casting is on-point, with the small-framed and black-haired Levy to a nice visual counterpoint to Chlumecky's more athletic build and blond halo of curls. They, and everything else in this production, work together to bring a theatrical warhorse galloping into 21st Century Broadway, surprising us with just how much pluck it can still carry.
